courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Literary Fantasy and Historical Reality
courses.description: The intersection of literary fantasy with historical reality considered in two ways: (1) fantastic-looking tales based on historical reality; and (2) stories describing fantastic situations that actually came true. Previously offered as GERM 50.

source.text: GSLL 50. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-AESTH or FC-PAST.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Stalin and Hitler: Historical Issues in Cultural and Other Perspectives
courses.description: Critical issues that dominated the 20th century: WWI and Bolshevik Revolution; rise of fascism, Lenin, Stalin, Hitler and their roles; origins and evolution of Cold War; collapse of Eastern Bloc. Previously offered as GERM 51.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Nature and Death: Ecological Crises in German Literature and Film
courses.description: This seminar explores ecological crises and their depiction in German literature and film. The texts and films we will discuss will range from early Romantic fairy tales to present-day documentaries and climate-change literature (cli-fi). Together, we will face nuclear catastrophes, flooding, landslides, mass extinction, and climate change. Films with English subtitles; readings and discussions in English. Students may not receive credit for both GSLL 52 and GERM 255 .

source.text: GSLL 52. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-AESTH or FC-KNOWING.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Early Germanic Culture: Myth, Magic, Murder, and Mayhem
courses.description: Introduction to pre-Christian culture of Germany, Anglo-Saxon England, and Scandinavia from the late Roman Empire through the Viking Age, as preserved in myths, sagas, charms, inscriptions, and historical documents. Previously offered as GERM 53. Students may not receive credit for both GERM 215 and GSLL 53 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Once upon a Fairy Tale: Fairy Tales and Childhood, Then and Now
courses.description: Fairy tales from different national traditions and historical periods read through various critical lenses, against a backdrop of changing historical conceptions of the child. Works from Grimm, Anderson, Brontë, Disney, etc. Students may not receive credit for both GSLL 54 and GERM 279 / CMPL 279 . Previously offered as GERM 54.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Fantasies of Rome: Gladiators, Senators, Soothsayers, and Caesars
courses.description: Introduces students to study of humanities by examining how the idea of Rome evolved through poetry, history, philosophy, opera, even forgery into a concept that has long outlasted the Romans. Previously offered as GERM 55.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Germans, Jews, and the History of Anti-Semitism
courses.description: This course seeks to explore the historically difficult position of minorities in the modern world, using the situation of Jews in Germany from the 18th century to the Holocaust as a case study. Previously offered as GERM 56.

source.text: GSLL 56. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-PAST or FC-POWER. | JWST 56 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Moscow 1937: Dictatorships and Their Defenders
courses.description: Stalinist Soviet Union serves as a case study to examine how dictatorships develop and how they tend to be enveloped in justifications and kept in existence by outside observers. Previously offered as GERM 59.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Avant-Garde Cinema: History, Themes, Textures
courses.description: Students explore the international history, filmic techniques and cultural meanings of non-narrative cinema of the 20th century. Students also transform in-class discussions and individual essays into video projects. Previously offered as GERM 60.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Performing America
courses.description: The intersection of performance in a theater space and in everyday life will serve as a springboard to investigating the diversity of contemporary America. Examines how race, class, religion, sexuality, sexual orientation, history, and death are performed in America today. Previously offered as GERM 63.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Blackness in the European Imaginary, Europe in the Black Imaginary
courses.description: This seminar deals with how encounters between Europe and the African Diaspora have changed notions of race, nation, identity, and belonging in the 20th century. Through engaging with diverse texts--literary, nonliterary, and visual--we will explore the construction of blackness in various national and historical contexts. Previously offered as GERM 67.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Intensity, Vitality, Ecstasy: Affects in Literature, Film, and Philosophy
courses.description: This course focuses on three powerful affective states that challenge the conception of humans as autonomous, independent beings: intensity, vitality, and ecstasy. We will examine both philosophical and artistic representations of these particular states, focusing on the way in which they both endanger and enrich our experience of the world. Previously offered as GERM 68. Honors version available.

source.text: GSLL 68. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Laughing and Crying at the Movies: Film and Experience
courses.description: Why is it that we cry at the movies? We will focus on the melodrama but also look at comedy and horror to think about emotional responses to films. Students will learn the basics of film analysis, gain an overview of genre cinema, and study approaches to emotion, affect, and the body.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Teenage Kicks: Race, Class, and Gender in Postwar Youth Cultures
courses.description: This seminar investigates youth cultures from the 1940s to the present in the United States and around the world. It offers students a history of how different youth cultures developed over time, and consideration of how the constitution of youth cultures has been influenced by factors like race, class, and gender.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: The Book of Books: Literature and the Bible
courses.description: This seminar examines the influence the Bible had on great works of Western literature and traces this powerful literary tradition through different cultures and historical periods. Readings and discussions in English.

source.text: GSLL 75. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-AESTH or FC-PAST.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Uncharted Territory: Underworlds in Literature and the Visual Arts
courses.description: This course examines concepts and representations of underworlds in literature and the visual arts from the ancient world to the Middle Ages and Renaissance to modernity. Our journey will take us to the realms of the afterlife as well as into the abyss of the human psyche and the shady areas of underground criminal activities. We will explore how the desire to know the beyond has triggered people's imagination, inspired literary and artistic traditions.

source.text: GSLL 76. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-AESTH or FC-PAST.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Not Just Dogs: Animals in Russian Literature
courses.description: This course explores the question of the animal in the works of major Russian writers (Gogol, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Turgenev, Chekhov, Platonov). Among the topics to be discussed are: The animal as the other; animal and human natures: dominance and submission, ethics of human/animal relations, and the trope of "talking" animals. Readings and discussions in English.

source.text: GSLL 80. | 3 Credits. | FY-SEMINAR, FC-AESTH or FC-PAST.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Doctor Stories
courses.description: Explores and reflects on the experience and significance of being a doctor in Russia and the United States, analyzing "doctors' stories" presented in fiction, nonfiction, film, and other media. Previously offered as SLAV 82.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: We, Robots: Identifying with our Automated Others in Fiction and Film
courses.description: The word "robot" was invented by Czech author Karel Capek in 1920. Science fiction has had a long-running obsession with robots. Fiction and film dream up robots who have mastered and often surpassed the strange art that is being human. In this class, we will read and watch stories about robots from East and Central Europe, with occasional detours into American culture. Films with English subtitles; readings and discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Terror for the People: Terrorism in Russian Literature and History
courses.description: Terror was used as a political weapon in 19th-century Russia. This seminar introduces the terrorists through their own writings and fictional representations in novels by Fyodor Dostoevsky and Joseph Conrad. Previously offered as SLAV 84.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Children and War
courses.description: Readings for this seminar include children's wartime diaries, adult memoirs of child survivors, and fiction from Central and Eastern Europe. Previously offered as SLAV 85.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Literature and Madness
courses.description: The seminar considers the relationship between literature and madness through the works of major Russian writers (Pushkin, Gogol, Dostoevsky, Turgenev, Chekhov, Nabokov). Previously offered as SLAV 86.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Literature Confronting Totalitarianism
courses.description: What is totalitarianism? Can a portrayal of suffering, even death, under a totalitarian state, have artistic value, or must it remain only a political pamphlet? This seminar studies authors who reveal the crimes of totalitarianism, while also showing the moral strength and/or weaknesses of humans victimized by the totalitarian state.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Gender and Fiction in Central and Eastern Europe
courses.description: An introduction to the region, this course examines the role of gender in central and east European literature from the end of the 19th century to contemporary times. Course materials include novels, films, historical readings, and essays. Readings and class discussions in English. Previously offered as SLAV 88H. Honors version available.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Special Topics in Germanic and Slavic Languages and Literatures
courses.description: Special topics course. Content will vary each semester.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: "Game of Thrones" and the Worlds of the European Middle Ages
courses.description: This course offers a historical perspective on the adaptation of medieval culture in "Game of Thrones." We will focus on topics such as family, politics, religion, violence, gender, slavery, outcasts, knighthood, travel, heroes, myths, and magic. Readings and discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Christianity and Islam in the Middle Ages
courses.description: This course draws on a variety of cultural documents to explore both the conflict and cross fertilization between the Christian and Islamic cultures of the Middle Ages. Readings and discussions in English. Previously offered as GERM 218.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Popular and Pious: Early Modern Jewish Literature
courses.description: This seminar covers popular and pious literature written by and for Jews in the 15th to 18th century in German-speaking countries. Originally written in Old Yiddish, this literature preserved the popular European genres and nonfiction accounts of Jewish community and family life. Readings and class discussions in English. Previously offered as GERM 225.

source.text: GSLL 225. | 3 Credits. | FC-PAST or FC-VALUES. | JWST 225 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Central Europe, Medieval to Modern
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to the long history of Central Europe before the modern era. This region--between the Baltic and the Alps and between the Rhine and the Bug--was inhabited by a variety of people speaking Germanic, Slavic, Baltic, and Magyar languages. Moving swiftly through the chronology of major events that continually transformed the political landscape of these territories, we ask: how did premodern legacies shape the modern history of Central Europe?

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: The Division of Germany, Reunification, and Conflict with Russia
courses.description: Why was occupied Germany divided into two states after World War II? Were the Cold War and division inevitable? We explore these questions in two chronological contexts: 1945-1949 and 1989-present, with emphasis on the reemergence of Western conflict with Putin's Russia. Readings and discussions in English. Previously offered as GERM 254. Honors version available.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Germany and Cold War: Occupation, Division, Reunification, Renewed Conflict with Russia (1945-Today)
courses.description: This course investigates the central role played by the "German question" in the break-up of the wartime alliance, the emergence of East-West political blocs, the subsequent dissolution of the USSR, and the return to new Russian-Western antagonisms. Readings and discussions in English. Previously offered as GERM 255 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Ideology and Aesthetics: Marxism and Literature
courses.description: This seminar provides students with a general introduction to Marxist thought with particular attention to its critical importance for interpreting the role of ideology in modern literature. Readings and class discussions in English. Previously taught as GSLL 251.

source.text: GSLL 259. | 3 Credits. | FC-AESTH or FC-KNOWING. | CMPL 259 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: From Berlin to Budapest: Literature, Film, and Culture of Central Europe
courses.description: Central Europe was at the center of dramatic transformations of the 20th century: collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, rise and fall of Nazism, transitions into and out of communism, and incorporation into the EU. The course explores the work of writers and filmmakers who depict these turbulent events as they played out in the region's capitals (Berlin, Budapest, Prague) & in lesser-known cities such as Lódz (Poland's industrial center) & the borderland city of Lviv. Taught in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: How Does It Feel? Yiddish Literature and Emotions
courses.description: This course delves into the profound emotional landscapes depicted in modern Yiddish literature. Envy, rage, love, optimism, fickleness, all these and others will be our focus in this course. The study of literary texts will be blended with theoretical frameworks in order to achieve a comprehensive understanding of how affect and emotions are both portrayed in literature and understood through critical theory. We will read seminal works such as Cynthia Ozick's Envy; or Yiddish in America, which explores themes of jealousy and cultural displacement, and Uri Nissan Gnessin's In the Gardens, which thematizes love and existential despair. Taught in English.

source.text: GSLL 267. | 3 Credits. | FC-AESTH or FC-KNOWING. | JWST 267 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Cultural Trends in Post-Communist Central Europe: Search for Identity, Importance of Jewish Voices
courses.description: We will study how contemporary literary and cinematic works of Central European intellectuals serve as reflections on the everyday life of this region. Readings and class discussions in English. Films with English subtitles.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Springtime for Hitler: Jews on Stage from Shakespeare to Mel Brooks
courses.description: This course examines the roles and representations of Jews in the world of the theater from Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice to the present, considering dramas, operas, musicals, film adaptations, and films. Readings and discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: German Culture and the Jewish Question
courses.description: A study of the role of Jews and the "Jewish question" in German culture from 1750 to the Holocaust and beyond. Discussions and texts (literary, political, theological) in English. Previously offered as GERM 270.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Vampires and Empires
courses.description: The course explores the vampire's changing meanings as a travelling concept in the visual and literary cultures of Eastern Europe and beyond. We critically examine the vampire's role in illustrating and reinscribing power dynamics between historical empires and their former colonies and peripheries. The vampires of our course materials are self-contradicting metaphors expressing both the resilience of the disempowered and the obstinacy of traditions resistant to change. Readings and class discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Poland, Russia, and Germany through the Prism of Film
courses.description: Explore the relationship between Poland, Russia, and Germany from World War II until the present day, through films and readings that cover World War II, the fall of Communism in Europe, the Holocaust and the post-war situation of Jews, religious faith, Putin's politics, women's rights, and the current refugee situation in Germany. Film directors include Balabanov, Becker, Fassbinder, Kalatozov, Holland, Mikhalkov, Polanski, Wajda, and Wenders. Readings and class discussions in English. Films with English subtitles.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Close Your Eyes and See a Film: The Documentary in Central Europe
courses.description: Aesthetic experiment, agit-prop tool, and instrument of social critique: documentary film is a flexible form. In the Socialist Bloc, documentary was sanctioned by the state but often used to undermine state power. This course is a survey of Polish, Czech, Yugoslav and Hungarian documentary film. We will explore studio productions alongside home movies, amateur films, and art films. Does documentary simply record reality, or can it change reality too? Readings & discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: This is the Way: Literature and Philosophy, East and West
courses.description: An interdisciplinary exploration of Eastern and Western traditions through literature, philosophy, and audiovisual media. Classical Chinese, Indian, and Greek texts are paired with later artistic and intellectual responses to address enduring and contemporary questions of meaning, cosmology, desire, the good life, and creativity. The course compares methods from literary study, philosophy, and cultural history to examine how aesthetic form and philosophical argumentation offer distinct but complementary approaches to these issues across, between, and within cultures.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Music, Image, Text
courses.description: This course examines the relationship between text, music, and the visual arts, focusing on the way in which nonliterary aesthetic content may both mediate and call into question cultural values.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: A River Runs Through It: Cultural Geography Through Imaginative Literature
courses.description: This course looks at cultural geography through the lens of literature about rivers. After a brief survey of the world's major rivers and a short dive into the way environmental science seeks to understand rivers, classes are devoted to poems, stories, novels, histories, and even science fiction about rivers. Students engage in mentored research culminating in a substantial essay. Readings and discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: The Dialectic of Whiteness and Blackness in Atlantic Cultures
courses.description: Traces the invention of race, racism, and discourses of cultural inferiority/superiority throughout Western culture. What historical events created the necessity for racist thinking? How did colonialism and transatlantic migration change Atlantic cultures? Why did black culture become fashionable? Is the 21st century "post-racial"? Readings and course descriptions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Holocaust Cinema in Eastern Europe
courses.description: A critical look at varieties of cinematic representation and memorialization of the Holocaust, from those countries of Europe where it mostly took place. Taught in English. All films in (or subtitled in) English. Previously offered as SLAV 281.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Afropessimism in American and European Film
courses.description: Scholars of Afropessimism argue that we are not living in the age of post-slavery, but in the "afterlife of slavery" and that Blacks exist outside of the world, because the social world is held together by anti-Blackness. This argumentation has had important effects within Black German and Black European Studies. This course seeks to explore these philosophical claims, by comparing American films with European films that deal with anti-Black racism. Readings and class discussions in English.

source.text: GSLL 282. | 3 Credits. | FC-POWER or FC-VALUES. | AAAD 282 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Hungarian Cinema since World War II
courses.description: An introduction to Hungarian society and culture since the end of World War II through a selection of film classics. Films with English subtitles. Readings and discussions in English. Previously offered as HUNG 280.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Dissent and Protest in Central Europe
courses.description: This course examines cultures of dissent and protest in Central Europe, including student protests of the 1960s and the fall of Communism in 1989. Materials include literature, film, music, theatre, and popular culture from Czechoslovakia, East Germany, West Germany, Hungary, and Poland. Readings and discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: The Upright and the Toppled: Public Lives of Monuments in Europe and the American South
courses.description: Recent years have seen a worldwide push for emancipatory acts of iconoclasm: calls to "topple" monuments as emblems of social oppression. This course examines cases of contested and demolished monuments in contexts close to home (the Carolina campus) and geographically remote (Poland, Prague). If demolishing a monument can be a violent act, how might visual objects in public space exert their own forces of violence? Readings and discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Into the Streets: 1968 and Dissent in Central Europe
courses.description: Protest movements of 1968 are often remembered as one "planetary event." In Western Europe, protesters demanded revolution, while in Eastern Europe, protesters living under communism demanded reform. In this course, we will explore dissent and counterculture in Central Europe through the lens of 1968. Through film and fiction from Poland, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary, we will investigate the impact of the Central European '68(s) worldwide. Films with English subtitles; readings and discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Graphic Medicine: The Intersection of Health and Comics
courses.description: We will explore the unique possibilities of comics in the form of graphic medicine: namely comics that thematize physical and mental health. How do comic artists work through issues of trauma and pain? How do artists with chronic illness and disabilities articulate their experience through comics? This course engages with the Medical Humanities, seeking to bring together students of medicine along with students of the humanities to contemplate how we communicate physical and mental illness. Readings and class discussions in English.

source.text: GSLL 288. | 3 Credits. | FC-CREATE or FC-GLOBAL. | CMPL 288 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Research, Creativity, and Innovation in the Humanities
courses.description: This course serves as an introduction to research methodologies, theories, and the university resources available to students seeking to perform cutting-edge research in the humanities. The goal of the course is to produce a substantial research project. The capacities developed in this course as well as the project itself could be used as the basis for grants, scholarships, internship applications, or an honors thesis. Taught in English. Previously offered as CMPL 395H/GSLL 295H/ROML 295H.

source.text: GSLL 295. | 3 Credits. | FC-AESTH, RESEARCH. | CMPL 395 , ROML 295 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Special Topics in Germanic and Slavic Languages and Literatures, FC-POWER
courses.description: Examines selected themes in the history, culture, society, art, and/or literature of Germanic and Slavic/East European countries.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Different Lives, Different Voices: Social Perspectives on Second Language Acquisition
courses.description: This seminar examines the relationship between language learning and diverse social contexts, focusing on how culture, identity, and community influence second language acquisition (SLA). Students will explore theoretical frameworks and empirical methods, with emphasis on quantitative and qualitative approaches. Through data collection, analysis, and hypothesis testing, we will assess the strengths and limitations of these methods in understanding SLA's social dynamics. Case studies and collaborative projects will highlight the lived experiences of diverse language learners, encouraging critical thinking and empathy. By course end, students will gain both theoretical insight and empirical research skills. Readings and class discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: The Origins of Culture: Translation and Self-Translation in Hebrew, Yiddish, and Beyond
courses.description: What happens when the translator is also the author of a work? Such instances occupy us in this course, which is devoted to the role of (self-)translation in the creation of Yiddish and Hebrew literatures. In self-translation, everything is blurred: what is the difference between translation and writing? What is the origin of a text, of a culture? How can one conceptualize ''fidelity to the original''? And what motivates someone to write their work in more than one language? Through theories of translation, world literature, and comparative literature, we will try to understand the unique type of creation self-translation produces.

source.text: GSLL 435. | 3 Credits. | FC-AESTH or FC-GLOBAL. | JWST 435 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Literature of Atrocity: The Gulag and the Holocaust in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
courses.description: Historical contexts and connections through artistic representation of the Holocaust and Soviet terror in Eastern Europe and the USSR. Taught in English; some foreign language readings for qualified students.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Magical Realism: Central European Literature in a Global Context
courses.description: This course studies magical realism in Central European literature and film by placing it in a global literary/cinema context. Readings and discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Cultural Theory and Criticism in Eastern Europe
courses.description: This course is a history of cultural theory in Eastern Europe, offering students an overview of the major movements in the region that came to define theory globally in the twentieth century. The course examines both movements that emerged from the revolutionary politics of the Eastern Bloc and as well as ones developed by those who fled it: Marxism, psychoanalysis, Formalism, Structuralism, and semiotics. The course offers an overview of the East European intellectual tradition with works from Czech, Hungarian, German, Russian, Polish, and Estonian. All readings provided in English.

source.text: GSLL 476. | 3 Credits. | FC-AESTH or FC-KNOWING. | CMPL 476 .

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Grand Hotels and Empty Fields: Inventing Central Europe through Culture
courses.description: This course explores fictional inventions of Central European countries, from the mist-shrouded mountains of Wes Anderson's Zubrowka to the rigorously researched Orsinia conceived by fantasy & science fiction author Ursula K. Le Guin. We will critically reflect on the construction of national and regional identity and on fiction's role in this process. The course is an introduction to concepts from postcolonial theory and critical area studies. Readings and discussions in English; films with English subtitles.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: GSLL Across the Curriculum (LAC)
courses.description: This one-credit hour class aims to develop and facilitate conversational skills in a Germanic or Slavic language in the context of the current political, economic, and cultural climate. Knowledge of the language of instruction at the upper-intermediate level required.
courses.requisites_raw: Prerequisite, BCS 404, CZCH 404, DTCH 404, GERM 204, HUNG 404, KAZH 404, PLSH 404, RUSS 204, or UKRN 404; permission of instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 6 total credits. 6 total completions.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Topics in Germanic and Slavic Languages and Literatures
courses.description: Examines selected themes in the history, culture, society, art, and/or literature of Germanic and Slavic/East European countries.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Weaponization of Knowledge: Historical Legacy of Propaganda and Disinformation in the US and Abroad
courses.description: Thomas Jefferson believed a stable democracy requires an informed citizenry. But how do we think about the relationship between knowledge and power? In this class, we will explore how those in power create knowledge and understand how what counts as knowledge is used to maintain their political position. By learning sociological frameworks to question knowledge and reality, this class will then use that theory to study applied cases of weaponized knowledge throughout history in the United States and Germany. Students will learn foundational concepts, and develop an array of communication strategies for distinct situations and specific audiences. Taught in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Diversity in the European Union
courses.description: In this course, students will learn to conduct close readings of a variety of media, ranging from essays, novels, and poems to films and a musical, which all depict diverse populations in the EU and various Member States, including Spain, France, Italy, Germany, and the Netherlands. Examining the specific topic of Diversity in the EU, this course will give students the theoretical tools and historical context to engage with intersecting issues such as race, gender and class, religion, disability, citizenship, and immigration. Readings and class discussions in English.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Mentored Research
courses.description: In this course, students will carry out a research project under the direct supervision of a faculty mentor. The course culminates in a final research paper at the end of the semester.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Directed Readings
courses.description: In this course, students work through a reading list in a specific field under the direction of a faculty member. Permission of the instructor required.
courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Reading Other Cultures: Issues in Literary Translation
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. Reading knowledge of a language other than English recommended. Starting from the proposition that cultural literacy would be impossible without reliance on translations, this course addresses fundamental issues in the practice, art, and politics of literary translation. Previously offered as SLAV 560.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: From Information Theory to AI: What Was the Digital?
courses.description: We live, by all accounts, in a digital age. Technological devices and infrastructures like smartphones, the internet, social media, and artificial intelligence have come to shape virtually every domain of our daily experience and deeply influence the ways in which we think, act, and understand the world. But how did ''the digital'' actually develop into the omnipresent phenomenon and catchword it is today? When and where did it initially emerge and how was it conceptualized over time by theorists, scientists, philosophers, artists, and writers? This course explores the history of digital culture and theory from the 1940s to the present.

courses.subject: GSLL
courses.title: Moving-Image Avant-gardes and Experimentalism
courses.description: History and theory of international avant-garde and experimentalist movements in film, video, intermedia, multimedia, and digital formats. Content and focus may vary from semester to semester. Readings and class discussions in English. Previously offered as GERM 683.
courses.requisites_raw: Prerequisite, ARTH 159, COMM 140, or ENGL 142; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

items.text: permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite

courses.repeat_rules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.
